# STARC Institute (星弧)

> STARC Institute (Chinese name 星弧) is a small nonprofit that helps university students build real products and do real research, as an alternative to pay-to-play research programs and résumé packages (背景提升) that sell the appearance of experience.

Key facts:
- Main program: the One-Person Company (OPC, 一人公司计划) cohort. 12 students, 8 weeks, about 10 hours a week. Each student builds and launches a real product with AI tools, finds real users, and keeps a weekly build log. For undergraduate and master's students, any major. Apply through the application form: https://forms.gle/9kHxzd7byt3BKD2k9
- Graduation is judged by evidence (a live product, real usage data, eight build logs), not by a certificate. Two outcomes: Shipped (at least 10 real external users) and Completed (full participation, fewer users).
- Selective research track (科研合作): rare openings with an active researcher; publication is never promised.
- STARC does not ghost-write, does not guarantee outcomes, and does not sell recommendation letters or authorship.
- Applications are reviewed with school names removed.
- The team is small; names are not listed yet.

## Blog: questions answered
- [Can I talk about a project I built with AI in a grad school interview?](https://starc.institute/blog/ai-project-grad-school-interview.html): Yes, you can talk about a project you built with AI in a grad school interview, as long as you can explain every decision in it yourself. Faculty interviewers aren't checking whether you typed each line. They're checking whether you can define a problem, make trade-offs, test your own work and say honestly what didn't work. Be plain about what AI did and specific about what you decided.
- [Do students from less well-known universities stand a chance in a blind-reviewed program?](https://starc.institute/blog/blind-review-less-known-university.html): Yes, if the review is truly blind and the application asks for things any student can produce. A blind review hides the school name, so what's left to judge is the work you submit. It does not erase every advantage, so the best strategy is to send something a reviewer can open and check, such as a live project and an honest account of how you built it.
- [What's the difference between a student one-person company program and an AI side hustle course?](https://starc.institute/blog/one-person-company-vs-ai-side-hustle.html): A student one-person company program is judged by what you ship: a live product, real users and an honest record of how you built it. An AI side hustle course is judged by what it sells you: lessons, templates and a promise of income, often followed by a pricier next course. The quickest test is to ask who earns money if things go well, and what you will have to show at the end that someone can open and check.
- [Are there nonprofit research mentorship options for undergraduates?](https://starc.institute/blog/nonprofit-research-mentorship-undergraduates.html): Yes, and most of them don't advertise. The biggest are NSF-funded REU summer programs, which pay participants rather than charging them, your own university's undergraduate research office, and joining a professor's lab directly. Small independent nonprofits exist too, but judge any program by its written rules, not by the word "nonprofit".
- [Can I build a real product with AI if I can't code?](https://starc.institute/blog/build-product-with-ai-without-coding.html): Yes. AI coding assistants now let a non-programmer build and launch a small, working web product, as long as the problem is narrow and you're willing to read error messages and test everything yourself. The hard part was never typing code. It's choosing a real problem, finding users, and judging whether what the AI produced actually works.
- [Are paid research internships worth it?](https://starc.institute/blog/are-paid-research-internships-worth-it.html): Sometimes, but far less often than the price suggests. A paid program is worth considering only if you'll do real work on a real question with an active researcher, and they'll tell you plainly what you will and won't get. If a program promises a publication, an admission advantage or a recommendation letter in exchange for a fee, treat that as a warning sign, not a feature.
